section_summary: This section is dominated by congressional and industrial protests against exporting scrap iron to Japan, together with State Department replies explaining the export-licensing system established under the Export Control Act and the presidential proclamations of July 2 and July 26, 1940. It also documents the Yugoslav vessel BOR carrying scrap iron from Puerto Rico and Colombia toward Japan, and includes an unrelated request concerning cotton-linter export licenses. The final pages contain confidential FBI correspondence and a detailed investigation of efforts by Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha representatives and intermediaries to purchase large quantities of American aviation gasoline, allegedly for the Japanese Navy.

subfiles.title: Copy report on the BOR scrap-iron shipment at Puerto Colombia
subfiles.from: Phelan
subfiles.about: Reports the arrival and planned loading of the Yugoslav vessel BOR with scrap iron at Puerto Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Report on the BOR at Puerto Colombia: about 3,100 tons of scrap aboard, 2,700-3,000 more to load, a multinational crew, and a possible labor dispute over boxed cargo.

subfiles.title: Ashurst office referral of scrap-iron protest
subfiles.from: Office of Senator Henry F. Ashurst
subfiles.about: Refers an enclosed constituent communication concerning scrap-iron exports for State Department consideration and report.
subfiles.summary: Senator Ashurst's office forwards a scrap-iron protest to State, requesting favorable consideration and a report.

subfiles.title: Telegram protesting proposed export of 300,000 tons of scrap iron
subfiles.from: E. C. Voss, Capitol Foundry Company
subfiles.about: Urges Senator Ashurst to oppose a proposed 300,000-ton scrap-iron export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Voss telegram protests a proposed 300,000-ton scrap-iron export as worsening a domestic shortage in the emergency and burdening iron and steel consumers.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Ashurst
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that iron and steel scrap exports now require licenses under the July 1940 export-control measures.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Ashurst's forwarding of E. C. Voss's telegram and encloses copies of the July 26 proclamation and regulations. He states that licensing decisions are governed by directives from the Administrator of Export Control and returns the constituent telegram.

subfiles.title: Ward letter forwarding Rustless Iron and Steel protest
subfiles.from: Representative David J. Ward
subfiles.about: Forwards a Baltimore steel company's protest against exporting 300,000 tons of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ward forwards a Rustless Iron and Steel telegram and asks the Department's advice and its return.

subfiles.title: Rustless Iron and Steel Corporation telegram to David J. Ward
subfiles.from: Rustless Iron and Steel Corporation
subfiles.about: Protests government approval of negotiations to export 300,000 tons of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rustless Iron and Steel asks Ward's help defeating the shipment as aggravating a shortage in the national emergency.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to David J. Ward
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Rustless Iron and Steel protest by describing the new export-license requirement.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the July 26 proclamation and regulations issued under the Export Control Act. He notes that iron and steel scrap are now licensed commodities and that the Administrator of Export Control directs action on applications; the telegram is returned.

subfiles.title: Cole letter forwarding Rustless Iron and Steel telegram
subfiles.from: Representative William P. Cole Jr.
subfiles.about: Requests information about contemplated action on the shipment of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cole forwards the Rustless telegram, inclined to agree, and asks what action is contemplated.

subfiles.title: Rustless Iron and Steel Corporation telegram to William P. Cole Jr.
subfiles.from: Rustless Iron and Steel Corporation
subfiles.about: Seeks congressional opposition to the pending export of 300,000 tons of scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rustless telegram to Cole warning the export would increase a shortage and burden domestic producers.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William P. Cole Jr.
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Describes the new export-control rules governing iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges the Rustless Iron and Steel telegram and encloses the July 26 proclamation and regulations. He explains that licenses are now required and that the Administrator of Export Control governs their disposition; the original telegram is returned.

subfiles.title: Overton Brooks letter reporting Louisiana protests
subfiles.from: Representative Overton Brooks
subfiles.about: Reports constituent opposition to selling scrap iron to Japan and requests the State Department's response.
subfiles.summary: Brooks quotes a telegram from G. B. Hall of the DeSoto Foundry & Machine Company stating that scrap is needed in the United States. He adds that other constituents view Japan as hostile and fear American scrap may later be used against the United States.

subfiles.title: Referral of Brooks letter to the Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Overton Brooks's protest letter to the export-control administrator.
subfiles.summary: Yost refers Brooks's letter to the Export Control Administrator, and Brooks has been informed.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Overton Brooks
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that scrap-metal exports require licenses and that Brooks's letter has been sent to the Administrator of Export Control.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Overton Brooks the Export Control Administrator decides licenses, so his letter and G. B. Hall's protest went to him, with the July 26 proclamation enclosed.

subfiles.title: Harter letter quoting Buffalo foundry protests
subfiles.from: Representative J. Francis Harter
subfiles.about: Reports Buffalo foundries' complaints of scrap shortages and asks what the government is doing about exports.
subfiles.summary: Harter quotes Buffalo foundries' protests of high spot prices and unavailable contracts and asks about the shortage and government action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. Francis Harter
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains how the new export-control system can restrict or prohibit scrap exports for national defense.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses three sets of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He states that the issue is under continuous government review and that licensing permits exports to be curtailed or prohibited whenever national defense requires it.

subfiles.title: Sasscer transmittal of Levering Brothers letter
subfiles.from: Representative Lansdale G. Sasscer
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter from Levering Brothers president J. P. Wade Levering.
subfiles.summary: Sasscer transmits Levering Brothers' letter on exporting scrap iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: Levering Brothers protest against scrap sale to Japan
subfiles.from: J. P. Wade Levering, President, Levering Brothers
subfiles.about: Argues that exporting 300,000 tons of scarce scrap iron to Japan would harm American rearmament.
subfiles.summary: Levering says scrap is one of his firm's two essential raw materials and already scarce; exporting it arms potential enemies while depriving American rearmament.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lansdale G. Sasscer
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Levering's protest with an explanation of scrap-export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses duplicate copies of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He says the new system permits curtailment or prohibition of scrap exports when required for national defense and returns Levering's letter.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the BOR's departure for Japan
subfiles.from: Nelson R. Park, American Consul, Barranquilla
subfiles.about: Reports the BOR's departure with scrap iron and describes its crew, visitors, and charterer's representative.
subfiles.summary: Park reports the BOR sailed for Japan with 5,780 tons of scrap via Cristobal and Hawaii, notes the captain, a German seaman, a Nazi leader's visit and charterer's representative Deutsch; Panama and Bogota embassies notified.

subfiles.title: Wiley transmittal of C. A. Lawton Company protest
subfiles.from: Senator Alexander Wiley
subfiles.about: Forwards E. W. Lawton's protest against exporting scrap iron to Japan and asks for a report.
subfiles.summary: Wiley forwards a C. A. Lawton Company protest, asking its return and a report to answer Lawton.

subfiles.title: C. A. Lawton Company protest
subfiles.from: E. W. Lawton, C. A. Lawton Company
subfiles.about: Protests exporting scarce scrap to Japan and warns that it could become enemy war equipment.
subfiles.summary: Lawton says the U.S. needs its increasingly scarce scrap and asks Wiley to stop exports that could enhance a future enemy's military capacity.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Wiley on Lawton protest
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the licensing system for iron and steel scrap and returns Lawton's letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses duplicate copies of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He states that the new controls permit the government to curtail or prohibit scrap exports in the interest of national defense and returns the constituent letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to export regulations file
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State records office
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of item 894.24/995 to the export-regulations file.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains only a records-management instruction. It states that the item was transferred to decimal file 811.20(D), Regulations/406.

subfiles.title: Overton letter forwarding Baird telegram
subfiles.from: Senator John H. Overton
subfiles.about: Requests a report explaining the new scrap-export licensing provisions to constituent J. Pat Baird.
subfiles.summary: Overton forwards Baird's telegram opposing exporting 300,000 tons of scrap iron and asks the Department to explain the new licensing and its likely effect.

subfiles.title: Memphis Cotton Linter Company request for export licenses
subfiles.from: Memphis Cotton Linter Company
subfiles.about: Seeks prompt issuance of export licenses for three railcars of cotton linters bound for Canada.
subfiles.summary: Memphis Cotton Linter Company lists overdue shipments to Canada and asks Davis to find when Leonard Price will issue export licenses.

subfiles.title: J. Pat Baird telegram opposing scrap exports
subfiles.from: J. Pat Baird, J. B. Baird Corporation
subfiles.about: Solicits Overton's support against the sale and export of 300,000 tons of scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. Pat Baird calls scrap a national resource essential to American users and says exporting it burdens domestic producers and consumers.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Overton
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the effect of the July 26 proclamation and refers the Baird protest to the Administrator of Export Control.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that, effective August 1, each exportation of iron and steel scrap requires a State Department license. He encloses the proclamation and regulations, returns the telegram, and forwards copies of Overton's letter and Baird's message to the Administrator responsible for final licensing decisions.

subfiles.title: Schwellenbach letter forwarding Bellingham Iron Works telegram
subfiles.from: Senator Lewis B. Schwellenbach
subfiles.about: Forwards a request to withhold 300,000 tons of scrap iron from export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schwellenbach forwards Bellingham Iron Works' warning that the shipment would damage domestic industry and jeopardize the national program.

subfiles.title: Bellingham Iron Works telegram
subfiles.from: T. Reid, President, Bellingham Iron Works
subfiles.about: Urges that a proposed 300,000-ton scrap-iron shipment to Japan be withheld.
subfiles.summary: Bellingham Iron Works telegram: the shipment would hurt American iron and steel industries and jeopardize the national program.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Schwellenbach
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Refers the Bellingham Iron Works protest to the Administrator of Export Control.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Schwellenbach the Administrator decides licenses, so copies were forwarded to him, with the telegram and proclamation returned.

subfiles.title: Wiley transmittal of Brillion Iron Works letter
subfiles.from: Senator Alexander Wiley
subfiles.about: Forwards R. D. Peters's letter about scrap exports to Japan and other countries.
subfiles.summary: Wiley asks State to comment on the Brillion Iron Works complaint, return the enclosure and supply a report for answering Peters.

subfiles.title: Brillion Iron Works complaint about scrap exports
subfiles.from: R. D. Peters, Brillion Iron Works
subfiles.about: Describes shortages and higher scrap prices affecting small foundries and urges an end to exports.
subfiles.summary: Peters says foreign demand forced premiums of $1.50-$3.00 a ton for scrap, small manufacturers may fail, and armament demand will worsen the shortage.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Wiley on Peters letter
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the government's authority to limit scrap exports and returns Peters's letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses duplicate copies of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He says the new export-control system allows curtailment or prohibition of scrap exports for national defense and returns the Brillion Iron Works letter.

subfiles.title: White House referral to the State Department
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Watson, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers Representative Rich's communication about scrap exports for State Department attention.
subfiles.summary: White House referral, signed by Edwin Watson, forwarding material to State.

subfiles.title: Rich letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Representative Robert P. Rich
subfiles.about: Reports the Sprout Waldron Company's protest against scrap-iron sales and exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rich tells Roosevelt scrap exports raise manufacturing costs and are inconsistent with the defense program.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Robert P. Rich
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Sprout Waldron protest by explaining the newly inaugurated export controls.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that Rich's letter was received from the White House and had already been acknowledged. He encloses duplicate copies of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations and says the system enables the government to restrict or prohibit scrap exports when national defense requires it.

subfiles.title: Capper letter urging a scrap embargo
subfiles.from: Senator Arthur Capper
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards four Midwestern industrial protests and urges an embargo on scrap-metal shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Capper says Midwestern manufacturers fear scrap exports will undermine defense work and argues only an embargo will conserve materials and end support for Japan's China invasion.

subfiles.title: Witte Engine Works telegram
subfiles.from: Edward H. Witte, Witte Engine Works
subfiles.about: Urges a halt to scrap-iron exports because of worsening domestic shortages.
subfiles.summary: Witte Engine Works says the shortage has worsened and continued shipments would burden domestic iron producers in the emergency.

subfiles.title: J. B. Ehrsam and Sons telegram
subfiles.from: E. H. Kuster, J. B. Ehrsam and Sons Manufacturing Company
subfiles.about: Protests exporting scrap iron to Japan during an acute Midwestern shortage.
subfiles.summary: J. B. Ehrsam and Sons, a scrap user, argues every ton shipped abroad weakens the defense program.

subfiles.title: Acme Foundry & Machine Company telegram
subfiles.from: E. L. Graham, Acme Foundry & Machine Company
subfiles.about: Protests the proposed export of 300,000 tons of scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acme Foundry & Machine's Graham says the shipment will aggravate an apparent shortage and burden steel producers.

subfiles.title: Sheffield Steel Corporation telegram advocating an embargo
subfiles.from: Sheffield Steel Corporation
subfiles.about: Argues that scrap exports to Japan threaten steel production, defense orders, employment, and national security.
subfiles.summary: Sheffield Steel says its mills depend on scrap, will make 10,000 tons of shells monthly, Japan already took over six million tons in ten years, and requiring finished-steel purchases would support American labor.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Arthur Capper
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Capper's embargo request by emphasizing the powers of the new export-control system.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Capper the system lets the government curtail or prohibit scrap exports when needed for national defense, returning four telegrams.

subfiles.title: Le Compte referral of Keith Furnace protest
subfiles.from: Representative Karl M. Le Compte
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent protest about scrap exports to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Le Compte's office sends the Keith Furnace protest to State, routed to Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Keith Furnace Company protest
subfiles.from: John C. Rehmann, Keith Furnace Company
subfiles.about: Protests exporting steel and iron scrap to Japan as harmful to defense and domestic prices.
subfiles.summary: Rehmann says scrap is needed at home in the emergency and exports reduce defense capacity, raise prices and are unpatriotic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Karl M. Le Compte
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the scrap-export licensing rules and returns Rehmann's letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses duplicate copies of the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He says the new controls allow the government to curtail or prohibit exports in the interest of national defense and returns the Keith Furnace Company letter.

subfiles.title: Treasury Department transmittal of Irene Edwards inquiry
subfiles.from: Under Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards Irene Edwards's questions about exports of war materials to Japan for an appropriate State Department reply.
subfiles.summary: Treasury transmits Irene Edwards's July 20 letter and its reply, noting the Japan-policy portion was referred to State.

subfiles.title: Irene Edwards letter on gold policy and Japan
subfiles.from: Irene Edwards
subfiles.about: Requests explanations of American gold policy, the Neutrality Act, and continuing exports of war materials and scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Irene Edwards asks why the U.S. hoards gold at Fort Knox, why it relies on a moral embargo while Japan wages war, and why scrap iron is still exported.

subfiles.title: Treasury reply to Irene Edwards
subfiles.from: Under Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Answers the gold-policy question and refers Edwards's questions about Japan to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Treasury encloses Morgenthau's explanations of gold purchases and forwards the Japan-policy part of Edwards's inquiry to State.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Irene Edwards
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act's application to Japan and the new controls on exports of scrap and other strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: Allen explains neither the President nor Congress made the finding invoking the Neutrality Act for the Japan conflict, admits substantial scrap went to Japan, and encloses the July export-control measures.

subfiles.title: FBI letter concerning financing of a Japanese aviation-gasoline purchase
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports a $20,000 payment connected with the proposed Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha aviation-gasoline purchase.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports Riggs National Bank told Crocker National Bank to pay $20,000 to Yokohama Specie Bank manager Motoyoshi on the Japanese Military Attaché's order, with intermediary Goldsmith unidentified.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of FBI gasoline information
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the FBI's July 26 information about Japan's purchase of aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Department thanks the FBI for confidential information on Japan's aviation-gasoline purchase.

subfiles.title: Hoover transmittal of Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha investigation data
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits investigative data concerning Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha and related persons.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle the FBI's Kansas City report on Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha's proposed aviation-gasoline purchase.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha aviation-gasoline negotiations
subfiles.from: M. B. Rhodes, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Kansas City
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation headquarters and field divisions
subfiles.about: Investigates a proposed purchase of one million gallons of aviation gasoline per month by Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha representatives, allegedly for the Japanese Navy.
subfiles.summary: The report traces negotiations involving W. E. Logan, the Hoss Oil Company, attorney Milton Cohen, Perry P. Schultz, Shoji Matsuzaki, and an unidentified Yamaguchi, with approaches to Phillips Petroleum and Gulf Oil. Investigators examined suspicions that Schultz might be connected to Germany, financial transfers through the Yokohama Specie Bank, the representatives' movements between Los Angeles, Detroit, Pittsburgh, Kansas City, and New York, and conflicting reports about whether Gulf had agreed to sell 20,000 drums. No German connection was established, the supposed $500,000 letter of credit was contradicted by bank records, and Logan's brokerage role collapsed when the buyers allegedly decided to deal directly with Gulf. The report assigns further investigative leads to the New York, Washington, Oklahoma City, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh, and Kansas City offices.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha report
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the FBI's July 13 transmission concerning Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha in Kansas City.
subfiles.summary: Department thanks the FBI for its confidential Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha, Kansas City investigative information.

subfiles.title: Hoover transmittal of additional investigative data
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits another set of FBI data for Berle's information.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle additional possibly relevant material; the enclosure lies beyond this section.
